messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya Patel had always taken pride in her eye for detail. At seventy-three, she still met clients at their homes, running her fingertips over upholstery swatches, noting how linen caught the light differently than cotton. But for the past three years, she had stopped touching certain fabrics without knowing why—a rough, synthetic weave would make her pull her hand back as if burned. She told herself it was just age, just sensitivity. But it was not age.

The event that undid her happened on a Tuesday afternoon. She had been driving home from a fabric warehouse in her old sedan, a bolt of velvet on the passenger seat, when blue lights flashed behind her. Two officers approached. She could not remember what they said. She could not remember why they pulled her over at all—her mind had gone dark at that moment, and the next thing she knew, she was on the ground, her cheek pressed against the coarse asphalt, a knee in her back, the grain of the pavement grinding into her skin. The uniformed arm pressing her down had a stiff, nylon sleeve, and the texture of that sleeve against her neck became a mark that her body would not let go.

She later learned that she had been accused of running a stop sign. She was not charged with anything. But the memory that remained was not a clean story. It came in disconnected pieces: the flash of a badge, the smell of sweat and synthetic fiber, the feeling of her glasses being knocked off, the sound of her own voice saying something she could not repeat. There were whole chunks she could not recover—how she got out of the car, whether she had argued, how long she lay there. When her daughter asked what happened, Priya opened her mouth and found no words. She knew what had happened. She had been there. But language would not come.

In the weeks that followed, Priya began to shrink her life. She stopped driving at all, because every police cruiser she spotted from her rearview mirror sent her heart racing, her palms slick against the steering wheel. She canceled a contract with a client who lived near the precinct. At first she called it traffic anxiety. But soon she was avoiding any situation where an authority figure might appear—she stopped attending community board meetings, stopped going to the bank after a uniformed security guard held the door for her and she flinched. Her interior design work suffered. She had always met clients in their homes, but now she insisted they come to her, claiming she had a stiff hip. She began working only with materials she knew well, refusing to sample new fabrics that had a coarse, rubbery backing. That particular texture—the one of the ground, or the sleeve, she could no longer separate them—made her queasy.

Her body had become an unreliable witness. She could be sitting quietly, reading, and suddenly she would be breathless, her muscles rigid, as if the danger had followed her into the living room. She knew she was safe. But her body did not believe it. She had come to believe that she could not handle even a minor disruption—a door slamming, a loud voice on television—without falling apart. And deeper than that, a conviction had settled in her chest: nothing good could happen to her anymore. The future had gone flat.

What finally brought Priya to a therapist’s office was a visit from her daughter, who found her mother on the floor of the study, shaking, unable to explain why. A package had arrived—a sample of a woven wallcovering from a new supplier—and when Priya touched it, the rough, grid-like texture had thrown her back into the pavement, into the knee, into the nothingness of the memory she could not complete. Her daughter made the appointment.

Now, sitting across from the clinician, Priya touches the arm of the chair and finds it velvet. She relaxes a fraction. She is afraid—afraid that recounting the event will break her open, afraid that she is too old to change, afraid that her body will never stop reacting. But she is also hoping, quietly, that someone will help her find the words she lost. That someone will help her touch the world again.
